title: SIAG/OPT Views-and-News, Volume 22, No. 1, March 2011: 'Integer and Nonlinear Optimization' (issue editor)
contribution: MINLP-themed newsletter issue edited by Leyffer. His editorial frames MINLP as a growing field with two strands: relaxations of simple nonlinear sets (Belotti et al.) and the minlp.org cyber-infrastructure for comparing formulations (Grossmann and Lee) (p. 14).
problem_entry: Editorial: the growth of MINLP as a field, shown by the IMA 2008 workshop, Marseille 2010, a planned third workshop and the first ISMP MINLP cluster in 2009 (p. 14).
key_idea: He sorts the issue's papers into strands of the field: tight polyhedral or conic relaxations of simple nonlinear sets, and an annotated public application library that promotes good modelling (p. 14).
experiments: none (his part). Belotti et al., not his voice: Couenne vs CouenneLTI on 474 instances including his MacMINLP, same machine, 2 h limit (pp. 5-7).
positioning: Presents MINLP to the SIAM optimization community; he is also chair of the Tseng Lectureship committee (p. 13) and is praised as newsletter editor in Todd's column (p. 13).
writing: A compact editorial that names each paper's role in the field and ends with a call for topical issues and contributions (p. 14).
limits_future: Plan to grow the newsletter from two to three issues a year (p. 14).

method_links.note: Endorses a public annotated library of applications where formulations can be compared; the test set of Belotti et al. includes his MacMINLP.
Weak: 'compare formulations' and 'good modeling practices' in his editorial.

transferable: When introducing a special issue, sort its papers into the strands of the field they stand for, so readers see the map and not only the papers (p. 14).
coauthors: none (issue editor); articles by Pietro Belotti, Andrew J. Miller, Mahdi Namazifar; Ignacio E. Grossmann and Jon Lee; column by Michael J. Todd

quotes.text: where authors study simple sets of nonlinear functions to obtain tight polyhedral or conic relaxations.
allows users to compare formulations, and promotes good modeling practices in optimization.

title: Optimal response to attacks on the open science grid
contribution: Read in preprint version ANL/MCS-P1593-0309 (2009). A collaboration-graph threat model for open science grids, with two MILP response models (close sites; close or monitor links) whose bilinear terms are exactly linearized. Solved on real OSG data in seconds, with a Pareto curve traced by sweeping the threat cap (preprint pp. 8-19).
problem_entry: Open grids cross institutional security perimeters, incident response takes 3-14 days, and no tools exist; entered through a new collaboration-based grid model from accounting data (preprint pp. 4-7).
key_idea: A linear fixed-point system for threat levels; binary site or link decisions maximize remaining utility under a threat cap. Products of binaries and bounded threats are linearized exactly, and the second objective is handled by an epsilon-constraint sweep (preprint pp. 8-13, 19).
assumptions: Threat spreads in proportion to shared load, with probabilities P0 before and P1 after detection, P0+P1<=1; monitoring discounts by 1-D; T0_i=0.1 in tests; Table 3 parameters (preprint pp. 8-9, 12, 15, 17).
proof_devices: Prop. 3.1: contraction condition gives threat levels in [0,1], by fixed-point iteration (preprint pp. 8-9)
Observation that link model 4.11 is a relaxation of site model 4.8, explaining its higher utility (preprint p. 19)
experiments: GAMS+CPLEX; TOY (11 sites) and OSG (23 sites, 253 edges), 1-4 compromised sites. Site model optimal in seconds. Link model failed at MIP tolerance 1e-3, solved at 1e-2 with ~11% gaps, up to 12,831 s at 5e-3 (preprint pp. 15-18).
positioning: Draws on grid-security tooling (GSI, VOMS) and collaboration-graph literature; cites MPCC literature to explain why the bilevel attacker extension cannot use it (preprint pp. 5, 21).
writing: Calls its results 'preliminary' and 'encouraging'; failures at tight tolerance are reported openly (preprint pp. 17, 20).
limits_future: Uncertain threat levels (stochastic or robust MIP), monitoring design, and the bilevel worst-case attack, called largely intractable at present because the lower level is a MIP (preprint pp. 20-21).

method_links.note: Bilinear binary-continuous terms are linearized exactly, giving an MILP instead of a nonconvex MINLP.
Failure at the tight MIP tolerance is reported, and loose-tolerance gaps are shown.
The MPCC route to the bilevel extension is named and rejected because the lower level is a MIP: the base cannot be carried in.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: epsilon-constraint sweep instead of a multiobjective solver
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Second objective turned into a threat cap; Pareto curve traced by repeated MIP solves over T_max

transferable: For a two-objective MIP without a multiobjective solver, cap one objective and sweep the cap; report the curve as piecewise constant (preprint p. 19).
Tighten the big-M linearization of binary x bounded-continuous products with the variable's own bound (T_j), not M=1 (preprint p. 10).
When a variant model is a relaxation of another, say so to explain its better objective (preprint p. 19).
coauthors: Mine Altunay, Jeffrey T. Linderoth, Zhen Xie

quotes.text: Unfortunately, these runs failed because of the large memory demand and long execution time even for the small test problem as OSG.

Clearly, the latter approach is less intrusive and provides a higher utility for the same threat level. This observation should not come as a surprise because we can interpret (4.11) as a relaxation of (4.8).

title: Concrete structure design using mixed-integer nonlinear programming with complementarity constraints
contribution: Read in preprint version (manuscript of 24 Nov 2009). An explicit MINLP with complementarity constraints for minimum-cost reinforced-concrete frames, solved to local optimality by MINLPBB/filterSQP despite MFCQ failing everywhere; 13% average savings over practice designs (preprint pp. 2, 21, 24).
problem_entry: Practice designs with a fixed initial stiffness, which is inconsistent with the final dimensions, so designs come out overengineered; earlier optimization fixed dimensions, rounded continuous solutions, or used GAs (preprint pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Integer dimensions and bar counts, binary bar sizes (SOS) and formwork reuse, FE equilibrium with dimension-dependent stiffness, inelastic steel and ACI factors as complementarity constraints written as nonlinear inequalities; nonlinear B&B chosen because OA/GBD/ECP/BARON need convexity or underestimators (preprint pp. 2, 5-6, 14-15, 18-19).
assumptions: 2-D one-bay frames with 1-8 stories, ACI/ASCE 7 loads, shear neglected; only local optimality since nonconvex; start from the practitioners' typical solution (preprint pp. 6, 16-19).
proof_devices: n/a (no theorems); modelling argument: fixing formwork binaries removes the nonlinear equalities 3a-3f (preprint p. 16)
experiments: MINLPBB, up to 678 variables (214 integer), 844 constraints, 120 complementarity pairs. Baselines: practice design, NLP root, rounding heuristic. 13% savings, rounding none; big-M and convex-hull reformulations 100x and 375x slower (preprint pp. 18, 20-21).
positioning: Extends complementarity-based inelastic structural analysis (Ferris and Tin-Loi; Horowitz and Moraes with MINLPBB) to full sizing with integer design variables; criticizes rounding and simplifying assumptions in earlier RC optimization (preprint pp. 3-4).
writing: Claims 'for the first time' an explicit MINLP formulation, names a new problem class, and gives an explicit solver-choice paragraph (preprint pp. 18-19, 24).
limits_future: Local solutions only; inferior local optima in the two largest free cases; tractable only up to eight stories; proposed fewer integers through grouped elements and a better branching scheme informed by a sensitivity study (preprint pp. 21, 24).

method_links.note: The MPEC-as-NLP result and MINLP-BB/filterSQP are carried into structural design, and the new class MINLP with complementarity constraints is named.

CQ failure is analysed (MFCQ fails at every feasible point), but the convex big-M and convex-hull reformulations were 100x and 375x slower than the nonconvex SOS and equality forms under nonlinear B&B: 'prefer convex' did not pay.
Practice and rounding baselines on the same start point; inferior local optima admitted.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Practice design vs NLP root vs rounded root vs MINLP solution on the same start; rounding gains nothing, so the integer model is needed

transferable: Justify integer variables by comparing practice design, NLP root bound, rounded root and MINLP solution from the same start point (preprint Table 4, p. 21).
Offer a 'fixed' variant pinning some binaries from domain knowledge and report its cost and quality against the free model (preprint pp. 16, 20-21).
Write a solver-choice paragraph naming which algorithm assumptions (convexity, underestimators) the model breaks (preprint pp. 18-19).

quotes.text: This approach gives rise to a degenerate MINLP that violates the Mangasarian-Fromowitz constraint qualification at any feasible point
However, the CPU time is about 100 times longer than that resulting from the special ordered set formulation for the three-story one-bay structure with vertical loads only.

title: Recorder Summary Research Needs in Multi-Dimensional, Multi-Scale Modeling and Algorithms for Next Generation Electricity Grids
contribution: A workshop recorder summary (Leyffer as recorder) of a session on multi-scale grid modelling: the paper's claim that grid physics is similar across scales, the discussant's call for network-aware HPC algorithms, and a discussion of data-driven vs physics-based models (pp. 1-3).
problem_entry: Reported: grid models span spatial, temporal and scenario scales, with renewables and N-k contingencies (p. 1).
key_idea: Reported, not his own claim: the physics of grid models is similar across scales and can be exploited in algorithms; needs listed are a consistent model library, multi-scale methods and uncertainty treatment (p. 1).
writing: Neutral recorder prose with bullet points; the paper summary, discussant summary and discussion are kept separate (pp. 1-3).
limits_future: Reported needs: consistency across scales, RTO coordination, weather resolution, EVs, scenario reduction for contingencies, replacing legacy code (pp. 2-3).

method_links.note: Weak; a recorded group view, not his own claim: 'be smarter about what we model'.
Weak; exploiting the shared physics across scales is the summarized paper's idea, not shown to be his.

quotes.text: Instead, power grid models exhibit similar physical models at the different scales, which can be exploited in the development of more efficient algorithms.
Overall, we need to be smarter about what we model, and how we overlap models, and transfer data between models.

title: Solving mixed-integer nonlinear programs by QP-diving
contribution: QP-diving: a nonlinear B&B that searches the tree with hot-started QP approximations built at the root NLP solution and solves NLPs only at QP-integral nodes. Finite and correct for convex MINLP; in Minotaur it beats BONMIN and Minotaur B&B on CPU time despite larger trees (pp. 5-15).
problem_entry: NLP solvers cannot be hot-started while LP solvers can; measured by strong-branching sweeps of NLP vs cold QP vs hot QP (Table 1) (pp. 4-5).
key_idea: Fix the Hessian and Jacobian at the root and change only bounds, so BQPD can hot-start during dives; the OA epigraph variable eta with an incumbent cap makes QP infeasibility a pruning certificate; OA cuts and positive multiplier floors tighten the QP (pp. 5-10).
assumptions: f and c convex and C2, X a bounded polyhedron; multipliers need only be nonnegative for correctness (pp. 3, 8, 10).
proof_devices: Prop. 2.1: finiteness and correctness by the B&B argument with two pruning cases (QP infeasible: by convexity the linearizations are outer approximations; QP integral: solve the NLP, then prune or branch) (pp. 8-9)
Remark: the subproblem at intermediate nodes is irrelevant as long as linear infeasibility is detected (p. 9)
One-dimensional -sqrt(x) example showing that a quadratic model can under- and over-estimate (p. 7)
experiments: Minotaur QP-diving vs BONMIN and Minotaur B&B with IPOPT and filterSQP (same IPOPT 3.10.1), CMU-IBM set, 2 h limit, failures coded -1. QP-diving fastest on ~60% with IPOPT and >=2x faster on 30%; trees ~10x larger; BQPD >=4x faster per node on 68% (pp. 11-15, 22-33).
positioning: Related to early branching (Borchers-Mitchell; Leyffer 2001) but a 'more radical break' that uses hot starts; cites Quesada-Grossmann and FilMINT for the cuts, Dolan-More for profiles (pp. 5, 10-11).
writing: Motivates the design with a measurement table before the algorithm; names three reasons for its own weakness (larger trees) in a dedicated section (pp. 5, 9).
limits_future: Larger trees, drifting QP approximation, BQPD reloads forced by filterSQP's static variables; future: QP updates, MILP cuts, QP interfaces without reloads, QP versions of local branching, diving and feasibility pump (pp. 9-11, 15-16).

method_links.note: Algorithm designed around the inner solver's reusable factors (BQPD hot-starts); OA epigraph trick reinterpreted as a QP pruning device; BQPD static-state defect worked around.
Same-solver builds, failure codes in tables, and an explicit statement of where QP-diving loses (larger trees).
A one-dimensional example shows the QP objective cannot bound f, which motivates the eta device.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: measure the re-solve cost before designing the tree search
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Table 1 strong-branching sweep NLP vs QP-cold vs QP-hot motivates the whole algorithm

transferable: Before proposing a new tree search, measure the cost of the subproblem re-solves it would replace (NLP vs cold QP vs hot QP on a strong-branching sweep) (p. 5).
When a surrogate subproblem cannot bound the objective, move the objective into an epigraph variable capped by the incumbent, so that infeasibility certifies pruning (p. 7).
For B&B variants, prove correctness by enumerating pruning cases, and state what the proof does not need (pp. 8-9).
Use extended performance profiles (ratio to the best other solver) so that values below 1 show by how much a solver is faster (pp. 11-12).

quotes.text: In fact, it is almost impossible to effectively hot-start any NLP solver.
The proof shows that in effect it does not matter what problem we solve at intermediate nodes as long as infeasibility of linear constraints is detected correctly

title: Heuristic static load-balancing algorithm applied to the fragment molecular orbital method
contribution: Heuristic static load balancing (HSLB) for GAMESS-FMO: benchmark, fit per-fragment scaling models, solve a convex MINLP for the core allocation with Minotaur, execute. At least 2x faster than dynamic load balancing, 80% efficiency on 163,840 Blue Gene/P cores (pp. 5-10).
problem_entry: Dynamic load balancing scales poorly for coarse-grained tasks of diverse sizes on many thousands of cores; fragment sizes are fixed by the chemistry (pp. 1, 3).
key_idea: Fit T_i(n)=a_i/n+b_i n^{c_i}+d_i, solve a min-max allocation MINLP in epigraph form; nonnegative fitted parameters make it convex so LP/NLP-based B&B gives a global allocation (pp. 5-8).
assumptions: Parametric performance model; sign constraints on parameters chosen for a highly scalable code; one SCC iteration is representative (p. 7).
proof_devices: n/a (no theorems); empirical check that different fitting starts change the parameters but not the allocation (pp. 6-7)
experiments: Blue Gene/P: Aurora-A kinase (155 fragments), HSLB >=2x faster than DLB; COX-1 (1093 fragments) 80% efficiency on 163,840 cores; allocation MINLP < 180 s on one core (pp. 9-10).
positioning: Positions itself as an evolution of DDI/GDDI parallelization; SLB revisited against the dominant DLB (pp. 1, 10).
writing: Engineering-paper style: a four-step recipe, practical recommendations (sample count >4, wide core range), and explicit operating limits (pp. 7, 9-10).
limits_future: Efficiency decline at high core counts from synchronization noise; HSLB applied only to the monomer step; separate data-gathering run; future adaptive HSLB with Minotaur called from GAMESS (pp. 7, 9-10).

method_links.note: MINLP machinery carried into HPC processor allocation.
Model shaped for the solver: an epigraph replaces the nonsmooth min-max, and sign constraints on the fit make the functions convex, so a convex-MINLP algorithm suffices.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: benchmark-fit-optimize-execute with convexity by parameter signs
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Fitted performance model constrained to nonnegative parameters so that the allocation MINLP is convex and extrapolates

transferable: Benchmark, fit a parametric cost model, optimize, execute; constrain the fitted parameters' signs so that the optimization is convex and extrapolates sensibly (pp. 6-7, 9).
Check stability of the decision, not of the fitted parameters, across fitting starts (pp. 6-7).
Compare candidate objectives (min-max, min-sum, max-min) and show the losing allocations in a figure (p. 8).
coauthors: Yuri Alexeev, Ashutosh Mahajan, Graham Fletcher, Dmitri G. Fedorov

quotes.text: The MINLP approach provides great flexibility in modeling the allocation problem realistically.
More important was the observation that the differences in parameter values did not translate into significant differences in the optimal allocation of cores that we calculate in the next step.

title: A pivoting algorithm for linear programming with linear complementarity constraints
contribution: Read in preprint version ANL/MCS-P1680-1009 (2009). A simplex-type pivoting algorithm for LPCCs with degeneracy handling, an anticycling scheme that certifies B-stationarity, and a two-phase start; finite termination; beats filter MPEC in pivots on MacMPEC-LPCC (preprint pp. 3-22).
problem_entry: NLP-based MPEC methods can converge to spurious C/M-stationary points; the Leyffer-Munson method needs LPCC subproblems; existing LPCC methods go through MIP or bilevel reformulations (preprint pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Active-set pivoting that keeps one constraint of each complementarity pair active and drops only eligible constraints; an extension set for degeneracy; cycle detection plus Bland's rule on each LP piece LP(x,P), P subset of D(x), to find descent or certify B-stationarity; LP Phase I plus a complementarity-repair Phase II (preprint pp. 7-18).
assumptions: Initially nondegeneracy and a given feasible vertex, both removed later; anticycling is exponential in the degree of nonstrictness, capped at 16 (preprint pp. 5, 20).
proof_devices: Lemma 3.1: termination with y_q=0 gives strong stationarity (preprint pp. 8-9)
Lemma 3.2 (Scheel-Scholtes): nondegenerate B-stationary implies strongly stationary (preprint p. 9)
Prop. 5.1: finite termination via Bland's rule per LP piece and a shrinking set U of unexamined pieces (preprint p. 16)
Minimal 6-variable LPCC on which Bland's rule cycles (5.1) (preprint p. 13); Scheel-Scholtes example of B- without strong stationarity (preprint p. 6)
experiments: MATLAB implementation vs filter MPEC on MacMPEC-LPCC (168 linearized MacMPEC problems), metric pivots, outcomes tabulated for both solvers; better profile also after removing the 30 unbounded problems (preprint pp. 20-22).
positioning: Works on the LPCC directly rather than via MIP or bilevel transformations (cutting planes, B&B, penalty) (preprint pp. 3-4).
writing: Modest conclusion ('an appealing alternative'); illustrative examples follow each algorithm (preprint pp. 9-10, 16, 22).
limits_future: Power-set enumeration limits anticycling; steepest edge and LU updates are said to be applicable but are not tested; the text says 12 LP-reducible problems were removed, yet Table 1 sums to 168 (preprint pp. 4, 20).

method_links.note: The classical simplex method is carried into a complementarity class rather than converting the class to MIP.
A minimal example shows Bland's rule cycling for LPCCs and motivates the anticycling scheme; the Scheel-Scholtes example is the test case for B- vs strong stationarity.
MacMPEC is re-used by linearizing it into the MacMPEC-LPCC test set.
Fair unit (pivots), failure categories for both solvers, and a re-run without the subset that biases against the competitor.

transferable: To extend an LP pivoting method to a complementarity class, find the invariant that keeps iterates feasible (one constraint per pair active) and restrict the leaving rule to moves that preserve it (preprint pp. 7-8).
Try a classical anticycling rule on the smallest degenerate instance of the new class; if it cycles, publish the example and the fix (preprint p. 13).
Build a test set for a subproblem class by linearizing a public library of the parent class and state what presolve removed (preprint p. 20).
If a competitor is handicapped on a subset for structural reasons, report profiles with and without that subset (preprint p. 21).

quotes.text: A common drawback of the NLP-based approach for MPECs is that it can converge to spurious stationary points, such as C-stationary or M-stationary points, with trivial descent directions.
Unfortunately, simply applying Bland’s rule to Algorithm 2 for LPCCs can still result in a cycle.
